questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working through the mechanism, which carbonyl partner with a Grignard reagent gives a secondary alcohol after workup?

options.misconception: a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol
carbon dioxide gives a carboxylic acid

questions.explanation: A Grignard reagent adds to an aldehyde to give a secondary alcohol after acidic workup, whereas formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol and ketones give tertiary alcohols.
questions.hint: Aldehyde plus Grignard gives a secondary alcohol.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Predict epoxide opening under basic conditions
questions.stem: Given the transformation, decide: where does a nucleophile attack an unsymmetrical epoxide under basic conditions?
questions.explanation: Under basic conditions an epoxide opens by backside attack at the less hindered carbon in an SN2-like process, so the nucleophile bonds to the less substituted carbon.
questions.hint: Basic opening favors the less hindered carbon.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A written test asks: which reagent oxidizes a secondary alcohol to a ketone without over-oxidation?

options.misconception: that can over-oxidize primary alcohols to acids
that is a strong reducing agent

questions.explanation: PCC oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones under anhydrous conditions, stopping before carboxylic acids form.
questions.hint: PCC is a mild, anhydrous oxidant.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Predict cleavage of an ether by HBr
questions.stem: In a review session, what products form when an excess of concentrated HBr cleaves diethyl ether?

options.text: Two equivalents of ethyl bromide and water

options.misconception: with excess HBr both groups become bromide
the ether oxygen is replaced under these conditions

questions.explanation: Protonation of the ether followed by SN2 attack by bromide converts each ethyl group into ethyl bromide; with excess HBr the alcohol formed is also converted, giving two equivalents of ethyl bromide.
questions.hint: Excess HBr converts both alkyl groups to bromides.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Predict epoxide opening under acidic conditions
questions.stem: A chemist observes the following: where does a nucleophile attack a protonated unsymmetrical epoxide?

options.text: Mostly at the more substituted carbon

options.misconception: the transition state is not symmetric
protonated epoxides are attacked at carbon

questions.explanation: After protonation the epoxide has significant carbocation character at the more substituted carbon, so nucleophiles attack there under acidic conditions despite greater steric hindrance.
questions.hint: Acidic opening favors the cation-like carbon.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A quiz question asks: why is a thiol more acidic than an analogous alcohol?

options.text: Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
options.misconception: sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen

options.text: The thiolate anion is larger and more polarizable
The S-H bond is shorter than O-H

questions.explanation: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, so negative charge is spread over a larger volume in a thiolate, stabilizing it more than an alkoxide despite sulfur's lower electronegativity.
questions.hint: Polarizability stabilizes the larger anion.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the sample reaction, which combination best avoids elimination in a Williamson ether synthesis?

options.text: A tertiary alkyl halide with an alkoxide
A secondary alkyl halide with a bulky alkoxide
An aryl halide with an alkoxide
options.misconception: aryl halides do not undergo SN2

options.text: A primary alkyl halide with an alkoxide

questions.explanation: Williamson synthesis works best with primary alkyl halides because alkoxides are strong bases and primary substrates favor SN2 substitution over competing E2 elimination.
questions.hint: Primary halides favor substitution.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: During a lab exercise, which group is commonly used to protect an alcohol as a silyl ether?

options.misconception: an acetyl group forms an ester, not a silyl ether
a methyl ether is not a silyl ether
a benzyl group forms a benzyl ether

questions.explanation: Bulky silyl chlorides such as tert-butyldimethylsilyl chloride react with alcohols to form silyl ethers that are stable to many conditions and removable with fluoride ion.
questions.hint: Silyl ethers are removed by fluoride.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a problem set, what regiochemistry results from hydroboration-oxidation of 1-ethylcyclohexene?

options.text: Markovnikov alcohol at the more substituted carbon
Anti-Markovnikov alcohol at the less substituted carbon
A ketone formed directly from the alkene
A vicinal diol formed by oxidation

questions.explanation: Hydroboration places boron at the less substituted carbon and oxidation replaces it with hydroxyl with retention, giving anti-Markovnikov hydration and syn stereochemistry.
questions.hint: Hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov and syn.

questions.stem: Testing your understanding: why do ethers have lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molar mass?

questions.hint: No O-H means no hydrogen-bond donation.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Predict cleavage of an ether by HBr
questions.stem: From the information supplied, what products form when an excess of concentrated HBr cleaves diethyl ether?

options.misconception: with excess HBr both groups become bromide
the ether oxygen is replaced under these conditions

options.text: Two equivalents of ethyl bromide and water

questions.explanation: Protonation of the ether followed by SN2 attack by bromide converts each ethyl group into ethyl bromide; with excess HBr the alcohol formed is also converted, giving two equivalents of ethyl bromide.
questions.hint: Excess HBr converts both alkyl groups to bromides.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Predict epoxide opening under acidic conditions
questions.stem: A mechanistic quiz asks: where does a nucleophile attack a protonated unsymmetrical epoxide?

options.misconception: the transition state is not symmetric
protonated epoxides are attacked at carbon

options.text: Mostly at the more substituted carbon

questions.explanation: After protonation the epoxide has significant carbocation character at the more substituted carbon, so nucleophiles attack there under acidic conditions despite greater steric hindrance.
questions.hint: Acidic opening favors the cation-like carbon.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Consider the reaction and decide: why is a thiol more acidic than an analogous alcohol?

options.text: The thiolate anion is larger and more polarizable
Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
options.misconception: sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen

options.text: The S-H bond is shorter than O-H

questions.explanation: Sulfur is larger and more polarizable than oxygen, so negative charge is spread over a larger volume in a thiolate, stabilizing it more than an alkoxide despite sulfur's lower electronegativity.
questions.hint: Polarizability stabilizes the larger anion.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Check your reasoning: which combination best avoids elimination in a Williamson ether synthesis?

options.text: A tertiary alkyl halide with an alkoxide
A primary alkyl halide with an alkoxide
A secondary alkyl halide with a bulky alkoxide
An aryl halide with an alkoxide
options.misconception: aryl halides do not undergo SN2

questions.explanation: Williamson synthesis works best with primary alkyl halides because alkoxides are strong bases and primary substrates favor SN2 substitution over competing E2 elimination.
questions.hint: Primary halides favor substitution.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a worked example, which group is commonly used to protect an alcohol as a silyl ether?

options.misconception: an acetyl group forms an ester, not a silyl ether
a methyl ether is not a silyl ether
a benzyl group forms a benzyl ether

questions.explanation: Bulky silyl chlorides such as tert-butyldimethylsilyl chloride react with alcohols to form silyl ethers that are stable to many conditions and removable with fluoride ion.
questions.hint: Silyl ethers are removed by fluoride.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: On an exam, what regiochemistry results from hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclopentene?

options.text: Markovnikov alcohol at the more substituted carbon
A ketone formed directly from the alkene
A vicinal diol formed by oxidation
Anti-Markovnikov alcohol at the less substituted carbon

questions.explanation: Hydroboration places boron at the less substituted carbon and oxidation replaces it with hydroxyl with retention, giving anti-Markovnikov hydration and syn stereochemistry.
questions.hint: Hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov and syn.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the reaction under study, why do ethers have lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molar mass?

options.text: Ethers have much larger molar masses

questions.explanation: Ethers have a polar C-O-C bond but no O-H group, so they cannot self-associate through hydrogen bonds, giving weaker intermolecular forces and lower boiling points than alcohols.
questions.hint: No O-H means no hydrogen-bond donation.
